name: Moxiong and dudou

lead: The moxiong and the dudou are traditional Chinese chest garments. The dudou is a diamond or rectangle of fabric tied at the neck and waist, and the moxiong is the Song-dynasty name for a strapless one-piece covering breasts and belly. They shaped how the torso looked under clothing and could also be an ornamental layer.
The dudou was reportedly used to flatten the breasts as well as to protect the stomach in traditional Chinese medicine. Today both appear in hanfu fashion and occasionally as outerwear.

paras: Worn as a layer against the torso, tied behind the neck and waist for the dudou. Fabrics ranged from cotton to silk and brocade, often embroidered with flowers or mandarin ducks. Modern hanfu sellers offer box-pleated, dart and plain moxiong styles.
Historic bust flattening was formally outlawed in Guangdong in 1927 after public debate. Modern garments are ordinary clothing with no special risks beyond fit.

angle.text: Historically the dudou was used to give a flatter chest line, and embroidered versions added colour and ornament. Moxiong are worn today as underwear or as decorative hanfu accessories.

lead: The dudou (also written doudu or doudou) is a traditional Chinese garment covering the front of the torso, tied at the neck and waist like a halter top.[1] The moxiong is the Song-dynasty name for a related strapless, single-piece garment covering breasts and belly, called hezi in the Tang dynasty.[2][3]

People wore these pieces to shape the silhouette: the dudou was originally an undershirt used to flatten the breasts and, in traditional Chinese medicine, to protect the stomach's qi.[1] Decorated versions also served as a visible ornament in hanfu.[2]
No studies have examined them as appearance tools. Their history is mostly documented through encyclopedia accounts, paintings and archaeological finds.
infobox: Single panel tied at neck and waist (dudou)[1]

paras: The typical dudou is a rectangular, rhomboid or diamond-shaped piece of fabric tied at the neck and waist.[1] Wealthier wearers used silk, yarn or brocade and the poorer wore cotton, and wealthy families sometimes used metal chains in place of silk thread.[1] Qing-era versions were shaped into diamonds that exposed more shoulder.[1] Red, pink and green were popular, with embroidery of flowers, butterflies or mandarin ducks.[1]

The moxiong is documented through Song-dynasty artifacts excavated in Fujian: a single-piece undergarment covering the breasts and belly.[2][3] Modern hanfu merchants sell box-pleated, triangle-dart and one-piece styles, plus a backless style based on a Southern Song tomb find.[2]

Wikipedia credits the original development to Yang Yuhuan, a consort of Emperor Xuanzong of the Tang, although the garment was then called hezi, and notes undershirt forms as early as the Qin.[1] The dudou became popular in the Ming from the mid-1300s.[1] A Song text tells a story of Yang Guifei covering a chest wound with a gold piece shaped like a hezi, after which court women copied the style.[2][3]

Small pockets were sometimes sewn in to hold herbs such as ginger or musk, and red versions were believed to ward off evil spirits.[1] Children also wore versions.[1] Toward the end of the Qing, European corsets and bras displaced the dudou, and using it to flatten the breasts was formally outlawed starting in Guangdong in 1927 after about a decade of public debate.[1]

Variations appeared in spring 2000 collections from Versace, Versus and Miu Miu, and some Chinese women, including actress Zhang Ziyi, wore it as outerwear, although many older Chinese disapproved.[1] Moxiong are worn as an undergarment or a decorative accessory in hanfu.[2]

timeline.event: Hezi garment associated with Yang Guifei.[2]
